speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: PROCEDURE TO BE FOLLOWED IN DEALING WITH AMENDMENT METHOD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the correspondence which has just been tabled between the Prime Minister and the Premier of Quebec indicating that the government of Quebec is not prepared to concur in proceeding with the amending formula known as the Ful-ton-Favreau formula, would the Prime Minister care to indicate to the house what action the government now proposes to take with a view to having a constitution in Canada amendable by Canadians?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: PROCEDURE TO BE FOLLOWED IN DEALING WITH AMENDMENT METHOD
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, the formula in question, as my hon. friend knows, has been approved by the heads of all the provincial governments at a federal-provincial conference. Approval has been confirmed by the governments of all the provinces but one, the province of Quebec. The Premier of that province has said that he is not willing to proceed with this matter at this time. He has postponed consideration.
At the moment we are giving consideration to this matter in the light of our statement in the Speech from the Throne that we intend to proceed to do everything we can to have the constitution of Canada repatriated, or patriat-ed. What is the best way to proceed in the existing circumstances? I do not know. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker-and we have been giving consideration to this-one way of making progress would be to set up a parliamentary committee.

maintopic: PROCEDURE TO BE FOLLOWED IN DEALING WITH AMENDMENT METHOD
speechtext: May I take it from the Prime Minister's remarks that the government has no intention of proceeding with the Fulton-Favreau formula unless there is unanimous concurrence by all the provinces?

maintopic: PROCEDURE TO BE FOLLOWED IN DEALING WITH AMENDMENT METHOD
speechtext: I think that would go without saying. Otherwise we would have brought this formula before the House of Commons for consideration in the last session.

maintopic: PROCEDURE TO BE FOLLOWED IN DEALING WITH AMENDMENT METHOD
speechtext: I wonder, since the government is considering setting up a committee to deal with the amending formula, whether consideration could not be given to broadening the scope of such a committee in order that it might deal with the whole question of a revised and dynamic constitution of Canada without confining itself solely to the question of amendment.

maintopic: PROCEDURE TO BE FOLLOWED IN DEALING WITH AMENDMENT METHOD
speechtext: I will be glad to give consideration to that question, but I am bound to add that if we cannot agree in this country upon a procedure for amending our own constitution within our own boundaries it might be difficult to agree on a totally new constitution.

maintopic: PROCEDURE TO BE FOLLOWED IN DEALING WITH AMENDMENT METHOD
speechtext: Does not the Prime Minister consider that it might be easier to arrive at a proper amending formula with the over-all picture than to agree on a formula which imposes a rigidity on something which is perhaps out of date?

maintopic: PROCEDURE TO BE FOLLOWED IN DEALING WITH AMENDMENT METHOD
speechtext: That is something which a committee of the kind to which I have referred might well consider.

maintopic: PROCEDURE TO BE FOLLOWED IN DEALING WITH AMENDMENT METHOD

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. Can the minister give us today some information concerning the delay in payments to the municipalities with respect to the winter works program?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: QUEBEC-DELAY IN PAYMENTS TO MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a number of questions were asked, one by the hon. member who has just spoken and one by the hon. member for Charlevoix, about this matter.
May I reply in this way. The federal government does not deal directly with the

municipalities of Quebec or of any other province concerning winter works projects or the methods by which these projects are being financed. The 50 per cent to 60 per cent contribution made by the federal government toward the cost of the labour employed on winter works is paid to municipalities through the medium of the provincial government. Consequently the federal government has no detailed information which would enable it to comment usefully upon the suggestion that Quebec municipalities are encountering difficulties in financing their winter works.
I have discussed the matter of federal grants for winter works with my colleague the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, and I have been reminded that under the arrangements made by the federal government to pay part of the labour costs of winter works there is a provision whereby the municipalities are able, if they so wish, to keep their interim financing at the banks for purposes of winter works at the minimum possible level so far as the federal portion of the assistance is concerned. That is to say, instead of waiting for the federal grant to be paid to them at the end of the winter, after the winter works projects have been completed and the municipal claim duly audited, municipalities may submit claims for progress or interim payments from the federal government up to 80 per cent of the amount to which they are entitled from time to time. Such claims can be paid by the federal government on the submission of a request by the province.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, January 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Goyer for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I wish to congratulate you most warmly on your appointment to your present office. In the short time I have had the pleasure of sitting under your chairmanship I have come to recognize the skill of a craftsman in the manner in which you are discharging your functions.
I should also like to extend my warmest congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address. As a new member myself I know some of the apprehensions, doubts and emotions that beset one in one's first speech in the House of Commons. I congratulate them not only for the content of their remarks but for the highly competent and self-assured manner in which they delivered them. I am sure this is in keeping with the best traditions of parliament, and I know they will represent their constituents with distinction for many years to come.
In participating in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak briefly on matters of trade and then say a few words about Expo '67, more by way of review and perhaps in an attempt to put it in its appropriate context.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
Yesterday my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) referred in his excellent presentation to Canada's current account deficit and some of the circumstances surrounding it. My remarks will be addressed particularly to our trade-a key element in our over-all current account-our exports and imports.
The participation of Canadian producers in foreign markets has both broadened and strengthened in recent years. Total exports increased by 10 per cent in 1963 compared with the preceding year and by a remarkable 19 per cent in 1964. Although December figures are not yet available it now appears that a further gain of 5 or 6 per cent was achieved in 1965. In other words, exports have risen by nearly two fifths in the three-year period from 1962 to 1965. All major commodity groups have contributed to this growth. However, the sharpest advance has occurred in the highly manufactured products
January 28, 1966

group. Automotive products have been especially prominent in this expansion, having increased fivefold in the three-year period. Substantial gains have also been realized throughout a broad range of machinery and equipment and consumer items. Farm products also have assumed greater prominence in Canada's exports in recent years.
Sales in each of the major market areas have risen in the past three years. Canada's exports to the United States have maintained a strong upward trend during this period, having increased by 13 per cent in each of the past two years. Imports from the United States have also risen sharply and Canada's trade deficit with this country has been growing. Exports to all overseas markets combined rose strongly from 1962 to 1964 but scarcely held level in 1965. Exports to Britain showed substantial growth from 1962 to 1964 and, despite import surcharges imposed by the United Kingdom, have held close to the 1964 level during the past year. Imports from Britain experienced no significant expansion from 1962 to 1964 but have shown major gains in recent months.
Nor is there any evidence of weakening in the strong underlying upward trend of Canada's foreign sales. Some unevenness in the growth of total exports has occurred, partly because of the irregular movement of a few important commodities. In the first nine months of 1965, for example, total exports were only slightly higher than in the same period of 1964. Factors contributing to this slower pace of growth included lower wheat shipments, the adverse effect of Britain's import surcharges and other restrictive measures aimed at correcting a serious balance of payments situation, and a slower pace of business conditions in several other important overseas markets. However, this slowing in export growth has proved to be temporary. New wheat contracts with Russia and mainland China, together with continuing strong growth in sales to the United States have given new impetus to export trends in recent months. Following the fairly level trend of foreign sales in the first nine months of 1965, the value of Canada's exports shot up to $791 million in October to record $924 million in November. Exports approaching $1 billion a month is very big business indeed.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
These figures are 15 per cent and 27 per cent respectively above the levels
The Address-Mr. Winters of the corresponding months one year earlier. Further substantial increases are anticipated in the months to come.
Notwithstanding the current healthy growth in exports, it will not be easy to keep the gap between external payments and receipts from widening in present circumstances of sustained and rapid growth within the Canadian economy. This is one of the problems which Canada traditionally faces in periods of rising prosperity. Imports have risen as sharply as exports over the past three years and the pace of advance has been accelerating. Prospects of a further substantial increase in capital spending in Canada along with steadily rising incomes will entail a continuing upward pressure on purchases from abroad. An all-out effort on the part of all groups in the export community will be needed to meet the mounting exchange requirements of our expanding economy.
In referring to Canada's growing imbalance, the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) suggests, as reported in Hansard of January 24, page 160:
If the rate of acceleration of 1965 over 1964 continues, we may easily find at the end of the present year that we have spent some $2 billion more outside Canada than we will have taken in.
While this projection is unrealistically gloomy, Canada's current account deficit, which probably approximated $1 billion in 1965, is likely to show some further increase in 1966, especially in the latter part of the year following the completion of presently scheduled wheat shipments to Russia.
I welcomed very much the comments made in this debate by the hon. member for Northumberland. He is one of a number of distinguished ministers who preceded me in this portfolio. I wish to commend him for a job well done during his period of enthusiastic leadership. In this debate he has made a number of suggestions concerning the trade promotional activities of the department and I shall be glad to give them careful consideration. He has advocated a repetition of certain programs undertaken while he was minister and the introduction of what he referred to as an agricultural trade crusade. The sorts of things which were undertaken to stimulate trade during that period were appropriate to the times and circumstances. He rendered a considerable service in awakening real interest in export throughout Canada and in bringing many new exporters into the field. He deserves credit for giving the morale of the department a boost at a time when it was needed. Circumstances have changed a great
January 28, 1966

The Address-Mr. Winters deal since those days and the department's policies have been reoriented and developed under the distinguished guidance of the present Minister of Finance. His contribution has been one of quality and foresight which has been recognized throughout the country. Like him I will be examining the current policies and practices of the department in the light of the needs of today and tomorrow, and the years ahead.
The world market is more and more competitive. We can now count, as was not so much the case in earlier years, on the active support and close co-operation in trade promotion of provincial departments of trade and industry. Today industrial and trade associations are increasingly active, and export trade is recognized as an integral part of more and more business organizations. The department's current efforts are directed on an intensive and selective basis to markets where particular new demands are identified, and to matching up Canada's productive and export capacities with these opportunities. Our export financing and export insurance facilities have been extended and improved. We are more active in the field of export education. Our trade fairs and trade missions programs have been increased and made more purposeful. Agriculture has been given a prominent place in the department's promotional work and good results have been obtained here, and also with respect to the sales of our fisheries products around the globe. The department is constantly refining and adjusting its trade promotional efforts to give improved and up to date service to the export community.
[DOT] (12:00 noon)
Selling abroad requires diligence, application, and teamwork on the part of a great many people. It is not simply a matter of securing adjustments in tariffs and duties. Our trade promotion programs and the best efforts of our trade commissioner service, excellent though they are, will not achieve the desired results unless we have the kind of goods that can be sold on the basis of price, quality and service, and it is on this matter of competitiveness I now wish to say a brief word.
Canadians enjoy many built-in advantages by virtue of our relatively favourable access to many of the resource ingredients that go into finished products. Our wages may give us some advantage over our competitors in the United States, but not in relation to many


other countries. To date, although our productivity is increasing, we have not yet reached the level we must attain if we are to get the export performance that Canada must have.
Some industries have demonstrated a high order of excellence, but there are still many areas in which Canadian manufacturers have a long way to go to achieve the efficiencies necessary to meet world competition. Productivity is the key to success. Every businessman is aware of this and I can only urge that the attention being devoted to this aspect of Canada's industrial life be intensified. In this the business community generally is dynamic and alert to opportunities.
I was interested to read last night where the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) was quoted in the press as saying-and Mr. Speaker, I hope you will excuse the words, as they are a quote-that he found business "duller than hell," and he went on to say "it is too easy, too polite, and everybody agrees with everybody all the time. Politics is a hopped up life." Mr. Speaker, we all know about politics; but I was surprised by his observations on business. The business environment in which he found himself must be considerably different from the environment in which the commercial and business life of this country is conducted. I know he is as aware as anybody else that it is far from dull if business is to keep abreast and ahead of developments, to meet a payroll, to seek opportunities on an expanding basis for the sale of one's products, and to end up the year with a favourable balance sheet. I think the hon. member would agree that that sort of business life is anything but dull.
The net difference between our external earning and our external spending, in other words the deficit on our current account, is made up by moneys flowing into Canada from abroad. There is, I think, a general apprehension about the degree of utilization of foreign capital in Canada, and it is true that much of our industry is owned abroad. However, I wish to make a distinction here that is well known to all, that there is a difference between ownership and the kind of financing that does not involve ownership. But foreign ownership undoubtedly has connotations perhaps over and above the economic realities.
Personally I would like to see a higher level of ownership of Canadian business in the hands of Canadians.

speechtext:
Hear, hear.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Steps have been taken to encourage this trend and, as Canada grows, and we have within our country more savings to spend on equities, I am sure Canadians will avail themselves of opportunities to increase their ownership interest. This has been the trend, as is evidenced by the fact that a number of companies in which a majority interest was owned abroad are now owned by Canadians.
But equity which controls the ownership of a company, and in which it is desirable to have Canadians participate more fully, is quite different from borrowing through bonds and debentures, and it is important that we maintain in this country a favourable climate for foreign investment in that form. Without it our development would have to be slowed very significantly, with attendant reductions in employment and other consequences. Nobody wishes to see this, nor do most Canadians deem such adjustment necessary in a country as well endowed as ours is.
It will take a long time, even with our best endeavours, to develop a sufficient surplus on trading account to bring our over-all current account in balance. That, of course, raises the question as to how long a country, or a company, can continue borrowing large amounts of money. Many dynamic and expansionist companies are in the same position in this regard as is Canada itself. They approach the problem on the basis that they can continue to accumulate debt as long as they have the capacity to pay the interest and otherwise service their obligations. The same, of course, holds for the country, but in due course the danger point is reached and it is a wise company and a wise country that can avoid this extreme.
Our trading account and our current account are, of course, the accumulation of the activities of all individuals and companies and governments. It is therefore important that all elements in this equation realize the circumstances and bend every effort to improve our exports, while at the same time keeping our imports within reasonable limits and financing in Canada as much of our development as possible.
I intend to keep in close touch with business and its changing needs, as well as with trading opportunities for Canadian products in other countries. To that end I have invited the trade commissioners in Europe to meet with me in Paris next month for an exchange

The Address-Mr. Winters of views and ideas. We will endeavour to leave no stone unturned in developing Canada's trading potential.
I wish to refer briefly to the Kennedy round of negotiations. Our efforts to search out and develop new export markets will be most successful if they are carried forward in a framework of expanding multilateral trade. For more than two years many of the world's trading nations have been seeking in the Kennedy round negotiations to give a new impetus to reduction of trade barriers on a world wide basis. The significance of these negotiations for Canada is illustrated by the fact that the participating countries account for more than four fifths of our total world trade.
From time to time there have been reports in the press about some slippage in the timetable for the Kennedy round, and problems which have arisen in some sectors of the negotiations, notably agriculture. More recently there has been a great deal of discussion about the implications of continuing difficulties in the European Economic Community.
Without ignoring the current uncertainties, it seems to me that there has been some tendency to overlook the ground which has already been covered in the Kennedy round. A great deal has been done to pave the way for the intensive bargaining which is expected to begin this spring, and provided the difficulties within the E.E.C. can be overcome, the outlook is for significant progress. Next month I plan to review the state of play at first hand with the Canadian delegation in Geneva.
It was never expected that this would be an easy negotiation. The objectives have been set higher than in any previous GATT tariff conference, and radically new negotiating techniques have been brought into play. For our part, we do not intend to allow our efforts and interest in these negotiations to be undermined by the delays and difficulties which are bound to arise in an undertaking of this kind. We intend to take full advantage of the opportunities offered by the Kennedy round to make further progress in freeing trade channels, and we assume that our trading partners are approaching the negotiations in the same spirit.
On Friday last the hon. member for Dan-forth (Mr. Scott) asked whether the government had received requests from Britain for co-operation and/or aid in curing its imbalance in trade problems, and about the nature
386	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Winters of the government's response. His question arose from press reports concerning an address to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in London, England, on January 20, by Lord Brown, a joint minister of the British Board of Trade. I have since had an opportunity to review the relevant portions of Lord Brown s statement.
Lord Brown referred to the nature of Canadian anti-dumping law and in this connection referred to last year's amendment to the Customs Act. This change was enacted to deal with certain situations where the British had represented that the valuation provisions of our customs law bore inequitably or unreasonably on British goods by comparison with goods from other countries, by reason of the quantities of goods sold or the trade level at which they were sold in the country of origin.
In announcing this change in the budget of April 26, 1965, the then minister of finance indicated the government's intention to use the new section 37A of the Customs Act to remove any discrimination of this nature against British goods.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
He added:
It Is the government's hope that this proposal will he taken by British exporters as a decisive response to their pleas that Canada give a clear signal that we welcome their goods; we hope, too they will respond by seeking out and serving' the very substantial demand which certainly exists here in Canada for imported goods.
As Lord Brown has said, the British authorities warmly welcomed the amendments made to the Customs Act. He has expressed concern, however, about the speed with which the amendment is being administered. A number of applications for rulings have been received by the Department of National Revenue, and a decision which will be of benefit to all British manufacturers of wire rope has already been rendered. Difficulties were, however, experienced in processing the other applications on the basis of the information supplied by the British firms concerned.
The house will be pleased to know that in order to assist, a senior customs officer was sent to Britain expressly for the purpose of helping the British exporters to develop the information necessary if full advantage is to be taken of the new provision. He has been in British for the past several weeks and I understand that good progress has been made.
We in Canada greatly value the United Kingdom market and our access to it. While 
DEBATES	January 28. 1966
an imbalance of trade is to be expected between a country like Canada, which is a supplier of raw materials, cereals and other foodstuffs as well as of manufactured goods, and a country like Britain, which is chiefly an exporter of manufactures, the government would welcome a greater participation by Britain in our expanding market for imports and a consequent improvement in their balance of trade position vis-a-vis Canada. The chief initiative in this regard must come from the British exporters themselves.
In this connection I have been most interested in the intensified promotional activities of the British trade authorities, designed to encourage a sustained and determined effort to meet the competitive conditions of the Canadian market and to expand British sales. These efforts, which are in many respects similar to the promotional programs of the Department of Trade and Commerce in Britain and other foreign markets, appear to be bearing fruit. British exports to Canada are up 5 per cent for the first ten months of 1965; in September the increase was 23 per cent over September, 1964, and in October the increase was 18 per cent-so the trend is strong.
Recently I had the pleasure of talking with Sir William McFadzean, Chairman of the British National Export Council. While both of us recognize that there are difficulties to be overcome, we are working to remove them. He expressed his satisfaction with the progress being made in British sales to the Canadian market.
Before commenting on Expo '67, I would like to say a general word about tourism because of the impact it has on Canadian trade, and having in mind the remarks made during this debate by the hon. members for Northumberland (Mr. Hees), Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Wadds) and Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse). My association with the tourist industry goes back to the days when I was doing my previous tour of duty as a member of parliament. This government feels strongly that more must be done at all levels not only to attract tourists to Canada, but to see that they find in Canada the sort of attractions and reception, accommodation and service which they seek and deserve. We must do more to ensure that each tourist who leaves Canada takes back with him an impression of his stay that will make him want to return and to pass the good word to his family and friends.
January 28, 1966

Our target for 1967, the centennial year, is tourist income of $1,000 million. With the help of all levels of government and from industry, we are moving at a good rate toward this target. The effort will have to be sustained and expanded if we are to succeed.
I will perhaps have more to say on this subject when the estimates of the department are being considered, but I can add now that in co-operation with the provinces and the private elements making up the industry, we are on the threshold of a concerted forward thrust toward the objective of realizing the real potential of tourism as a major contributor to Canadian prosperity.
Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks I should like to make with regard to Expo '67. In making these remarks, perhaps to put this great Canadian project in proper context I should review briefly some of the steps taken to date. Most of this information is better known to most hon. members than it is to me.
Canada's application to hold a first category universal and international exhibition in 1967 was approved by the Bureau of International Exhibitions in Paris on November 13, 1962. The Canadian corporation for the 1967 world exhibition was set up by an act of parliament on December 20, 1962. A tripartite agreement between the federal government, the government of the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal was signed on January 18, 1963, which provided for cost sharing among the three levels of government-50 per cent federal, 37J per cent Quebec, 124 per cent Montreal. This action was taken by the previous government, and once it was taken Canada became committed to a very high level of expenditure if this was to be the kind of creditable performance most Canadians would expect of a Canadian undertaking.
The decision to proceed with the exhibition was reaffirmed and the present management installed in September, 1963. This is when the project really got into high gear, so we can date most activity from that time; that is, when the management assumed its responsibilities. As required by the act, a master plan was produced and presented to the government on December 20, 1963.
Since becoming responsible to parliament for this operation, I have visited the exhibition site and the corporation office in Montreal. A number of my colleagues in the House of Commons and of the other place were kind enough to visit the site with me on January
The Address-Mr. Winters 22nd. I thank them for accepting my invitation. I have also had close consultations with my predecessor and with Hon. Gerard D. Levesque, the minister responsible in the province of Quebec for the exhibition.
The Canadian corporation is administered by a board of directors who are 16 senior business leaders and citizens from across the country, all serving on the board without compensation, other than expenses. I should also like to add at this point that the membership of the board comprises some of the most outstanding and hard-headed businessmen I know, and I am reminded that for a period of time the hon. member for Northumberland was a member of that board. The executive committee of the board is composed of Mr. Guy Roberge, representing both the board and the government of Canada; Mr. Andre Rousseau, representing the board and the province of Quebec; and Mr. Lucien Saulnier is the representative of the city of Montreal.

I do want to say, in order that hon. members will be aware of the controls that are exercised, that the act provides that the corporation's expenditures must be approved by the board, the treasury board of Canada, the governor in council of Canada, as well as the treasury board of the province of Quebec and the lieutenant governor in council of the province of Quebec.
The corporation operates under a master plan which budgets for all expenditures and revenues. Annual capital and operating budgets are approved by the board, the treasury board of Canada, the treasury board of Quebec, and the governor in council and the lieutenant governors of Canada and the province of Quebec. That is quite a gauntlet to run.
In addition, all expenditures of the corporation exceeding $100,000, or $25,000 where property is being acquired, require advance approval of the board, the treasury board of
January 28, 1966

The Address-Mr. Winters Canada, the Quebec minister on the advice of the Quebec treasury and the governor in council. I found the control procedures to be in keeping with good sound practices. It might interest hon. members to know that the corporation's operating procedures have been patterned on those of government departments and crown corporations and conform to the best practices of private enterprise.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
The corporation's purchasing is handled by the Department of Defence Production and its construction contracts are awarded and processed through Defence Construction (1951) Limited, so as to remove from the corporation the onus of undertaking these very heavy responsibilities. The National Employment Service of Canada and the Quebec Employment Service participate in recruiting. Therefore to the greatest extent that is feasible, Expo '67 leans on well accepted procedures and instrumentalities for service.
The government recognized when considering the master plan in the fall of 1963 that the exhibition faced a major problem in attracting skilled bilingual staff. Seven years of preparation were required for the Brussels Exhibition in 1958. An even bigger job had to be faced in Canada and only 3J years remained to do it. The Commissioner-General and the Deputy Commissioner-General resigned in the summer of 1963 and morale was then at a pretty low ebb. A major rebuilding job had to be undertaken on an urgent basis. The present management was induced to accept the assignment, but it was then getting late in the day.
The master plan set up an organization chart, establishment and salary scales which had been prepared and checked by the Civil Service Commissions of Canada and Quebec, approved by the board of directors and the two treasury boards and then by the governor in council and the lieutenant governor in council. With this establishment the corporation succeeded in attracting a high calibre staff-amazingly high calibre, in my opinion, from what I have seen of them-many of whom gave up successful careers and moved to Montreal with their families for this short term obligation. The staff was recruited from all parts of Canada, as was fitting for an all-Canadian effort of this character. The staff is dedicated and is setting a high standard in working in both official languages of this country.
Where does Expo stand now? When Canada undertook to stage a first category


world exhibition in the centennial year, the master plan assumed that it must be of high quality and that such quality would be necessary to attract the support of participants from Canada and from overseas. The wisdom of this policy is demonstrated by the fact that, to date, we have received official notices of participation from 70 nations, 10 Canadian provinces, one international organization the common market-one city, two states in the United States and 42 private participations representing over 800 Canadian companies. For the purposes of comparison, there were 43 participating countries in Brussels in 1958, compared to the 70 who have indicated that they will participate in our Expo.
In addition, the exhibition corporation is producing some 15 exhibits in seven buildings, and requests for space to exhibit are still coming in. The exhibition corporation is providing all the basic facilities on the site. In addition they have prepared concept designs for several smaller pavilions for prospective participants.
Good progress has also been made with the construction program. All major pavilions and facilities are now under way and the construction program is on target. As a control measure, the corporation controls the construction program through a computer-oriented critical path network system, in the best techniques known to industry. The exhibition is on schedule. Progress has been made with the advance sale of tickets in an outstanding way. I would simply say that when the same time had elapsed there were $1 million worth of sales made by the New York World's Fair, whereas there are now $10 million worth of advance sales for Expo '67.

Businessmen from all over the world will meet Canadians in this International Trade Centre and they will be encouraged to travel across the country to establish new business connections resulting from their introductions at the exhibition. Expo '67, in the eyes of the international business community, can put Canada on the map as never before.
Now I wish to say a few words as to the revenues and expenditures. I draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the very sizeable tax revenues which will accrue to the federal treasury as a result of the exhibition. These revenues are presently estimated at $46 million. There will also be sizeable tax returns for our partners in this enterprise, the government of the province of Quebec.

The services which the corporation is obliged to provide under the International Convention on Exhibitions have also increased as more countries and companies become exhibitors. Batten and Rinfret), as well as the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Messrs. Goyer and Stanbury). I congratulate them and wish them a successful career.

Every Speech from the Throne is subject to qualification, and so far in this debate we have heard it referred to in complimentary and not so complimentary terms. I was looking forward to a government program that would be, according to the terms used by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), bold, dynamic, imaginative and daring. Unfortunately, I was disappointed. In my opinion, it was sombrous, dull and soporific. Our main hope was for a daring program that would stimulate the imagination and give hope to the millions of Canadians who awaited these dynamic policies. These Canadians too were disappointed and resigned themselves to barbiturates to induce sleep and await another party that would set Canada upon the path of forming and introducing realistic and positive legislation to ensure the survival of the nation and give a realistic approach to the economic problems which plague us, from spiralling inflation to a shortage of goods and tight money policies.
Such legislation is absent from the Speech from the Throne and if indicated at all is couched in such words as to give it secondary importance. Next to legislation on capital punishment, those matters referred to above should have priority of study because the problems are not those that are to be feared in the future but problems which are with us today. The effect of these problems has meant misery to the larger part of our population. Inflationary costs are depriving our poor people of food, credit restrictions are threatening the survival of the small businessman and tight money policies, coupled with the high cost of production, are writing us off as an exporting nation. The future is grim if we do not face up now to these existing facts and adopt a positive approach to assure the survival of the nation.
The Prime Minister's declaration of intent to preserve the rights and prerogatives of national government are to be commended.

How seriously can this declaration be taken when we look at the haphazard direction we have taken in the last few years? At one time we have been approving a formula for amending the Canadian constitution and then forgoing that formula. Complete ignorance of the prerogatives and rights of the provincial governments has been indicated by proposing legislation in which the provinces are called upon to take part without first having consulted them on the proposed legislation. The Canadian federation has been under severe stress for many years. We do not seem to recognize some of the fundamental reasons. All the fault must not be laid at the feet of the national government. There must be coordination of effort based on an earnest desire for understanding and co-operation.
We must not allow ourselves to infringe on provincial prerogatives any more than we should allow the provinces to infringe on federal rights. Where both levels of government have rights under the constitution, a dialogue must be undertaken in order to understand mutually how best to approach the problem, to get the fullest value and to avoid wrangling and discord. The government must give direction, Mr. Speaker. It must also give leadership by introducing new ideas and formulas to bring our provinces, united and strong, under the one nation concept. It must not appear to the provinces that we are void of ideas and inept in taking the lead in all fields under federal jurisdiction. No more of these patchwork agreements should be evident.
My province might some day be Canada's foremost province. Its wealth and natural resources will be under the administration and control of Quebec people. All the recent attentions to Quebec have encouraged our younger generation to believe in the necessity of an education directed toward economics and the sciences but still retaining the goodness and fruits of a classical education. The economic level of its citizens will rise and they will enjoy equality of opportunity for positions in any commercial, economic or government field of employment. This is the hope for them, but let us agree to allow them to reach this goal. This goal should be accomplished, not to the detriment of other provinces but by mutual consent and by a constitution rewritten in Canada by a government which is aware of the aspirations of its people living under a system of provinces and a central government. The one Canada formula

Mr. Speaker, I extend my congratulations and express my admiration to the new Speaker of the house, to yourself, to the Deputy Speaker and chairman of committees, to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne (Messrs. Goyer and Stanbury), as well as to all re-elected and newly elected members who have come here to Ottawa to earnestly serve the Canadian people both in the house and in committees.
In this chorus of praise, I am not forgetting my genial colleague, the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) who earned the approbation of the public because of his personal qualities and his untiring devotion to public affairs for many years.
The Address-Mr. Allard
At the outset of this twenty seventh parliament which, unless it breaks up unexpectedly over political controversy or systematic obstruction, will preside over the centennial celebrations, we must ask ourselves what concerns should move the hearts and the minds of the legislators of our great Canada.
The Speech from the Throne shows two main purposes. First, the war against poverty within and, second, the political future of Canada.
I congratulate the government for emphasizing those two important problems and for having announced a series of legislative measures likely to alleviate them.
I understand that the present government will not limit itself to the legislation announced in the speech from the throne, but that it may suggest other solutions by means of the budget speech and through legislation submitted by the different departments. But, in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne does not go far enough; the government does not advance strong enough measures as appropriate solutions.
In fact, if we really wish to reduce misery, poverty and want in this country, we must not be afraid to strike at the very root of the unrest and to take immediate action.
As a general and practical policy, the government should have provided for a more democratic apportionment of the national revenue to further assist the labour and agricultural classes, and Canadians with low income.
To that end, it should revise the tax structure and set it on a basis which would take a greater account of families and social considerations. It should lower personal income tax for small wage earners who are faced with growing family obligations. In my opinion, the government should, in its next budget, provide a basic exemption of $4,000 for heads of families and of $2,000 for single people.
It is realized more and more that taxes foster the evil of poverty. It is becoming impossible for the head of a family with a salary of less than $4,000 to meet his obligations and face the ever increasing cost of living. When a man does not get enough help from the state, he is too often forced, in his distress, to turn to institutions and small loan companies which, without making judicious inquiries, further burden the family budget with excessive interest rates.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
In order to put an end to the exploitation of the small borrower and to make things
394	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Allard easier for him, the government should seriously consider setting a 12 per cent maximum on interest rates and raising the level of small loans from $1,500 to $5,000 at a 1/200 per cent rate of interest.
Family allowances should also be increased. We were very pleased to note at the last federal-provincial conference, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen), and several provincial ministers, agreed to review this act in force since 1945 and which no longer meets the needs and requirements of Canadian children, mothers and fathers.
The old age pensions will also have to be increased. I won't make a speech on the subject since an amendment has been moved in this house this session, but I would like to recall, Mr. Speaker, that refusal to increase old age pensions has been a great disappointment for many members and for many Canadians.
On this point, I should like to recall the recent statement by the president of the C.N.T.U., Mr. Marcel Pepin. According to this labour leader, the most significant failure of the present federal government is its refusal to increase old age pensions. Mr. Pepin, who represents thousands of heads of family and workers, also indicated the present level of such pensions is quite inadequate compared to the rate of economic growth of our community, particularly in view of the needs of old people.
It is all very well for each of us to rise and tell the government: You have introduced rather attractive pieces of legislation, but you have not done everything possible to meet present needs.
Of course, we all have suggestions which, at first sight, would lead the government to believe that we want to overtax its budget, destroy it or increase the deficit. But among the seven remedial measures I am pointing out today, there are some which, while allowing us to meet our commitments, would not burden any further the government's adverse budget and would not increase the fiscal burden already too heavy for Canadian taxpayers.
I shall point out two this afternoon. First of all, the government should seriously consider at this very session to reduce its military expenditures.
If Canada's appropriations for national defence are compared to those of other countries with similar national and international responsibilities, we find that they spend about

DEBATES	January 28, 1966
15 per cent of the total budget for national defence, while Canada earmarks almost 25 per cent of its budget for national defence.
I would like to quote a comparative table of national defence budgets for certain countries for the fiscal year 1964-65. Canada earmarks 24.7 per cent of its total budget for national defence; New Zealand, 8 per cent; Australia, 18 per cent; Belgium, 12 per cent; Norway, 17 per cent; Sweden, 17 per cent; Ireland, 5 per cent; Italy, 15 per cent; Spain, 12 per cent; Japan, 8 per cent; Czechoslovakia, 8 per cent; and three other countries, France, 23 per cent; Great Britain, 27 per cent and United States, 52 per cent.
As far as the last three countries are concerned, Mr. Speaker, it should be noted that, in the field of domestic affairs, they are considered large countries which entertain hopes of economic conquests and monopolies often supported by armed forces.
Such is not the case in Canada. I say we are operating above our means and we do not place correctly the priorities concerning the needs of Canadians. Therefore, Canada should review its international policy, restrict further its military expenditures and concentrate the greater part of its efforts on the needs and welfare of its people.
Another way would be to amend section 179 of the Criminal Code so as to allow the operation of national or provincial lotteries.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand why this matter has to be brought up every session, as it has been for so many years, when public opinion polls show that Canadians throughout the country want national and provincial lotteries. According to the most recent, held in 1961 I believe, 95 per cent of the people interviewed in Quebec, to mention but one province, were in favour of national and provincial lotteries. Such lotteries exist in many countries. They are to be found in Panama, Mexico, Australia, Ireland, Spain, and I could name about 30 other countries. That such a puritan attitude and contrariness should still exist is beyond me. To prevent governments, including that of Quebec which has wanted one for a long time, from holding lotteries shows a lack of vision. In 1935, the Quebec legislature unanimously passed an act asking that section 179 of the Criminal Code be amended to provide for the establishment of provincial lotteries.
That would enable governments to collect large amounts of money without having to increase the tax burden.

Mr. Speaker, I am proposing that solution to the government today.
We hear that the government had just set up, within the cabinet, a special program committee to co-ordinate the action of the federal government in order to improve the lot of the poor people in Canada, because there are thousands of them, not among us, but among the working and farming communities. The committee will see to it that the poor people of Canada-there are millions of them-take a more active part in the life of the country. I suggest that the committee should study the humble suggestions I am making today as well as those which were made by other hon. members during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, so that its next budget may be a pleasant surprise for all Canadians and reflect more vigour and dynamism in the political and financial administration of our country.
The second matter I want to deal with this afternoon concerns the political future of our great and beautiful Canada. Speeches from the throne reveal a growing tendency on the part of the federal government to take over responsibilities which the Canadian constitution of 1867 had not anticipated or had not granted to the central government. For the time being, I will limit myself to the field of education. In 1952, we saw the central government keep for itself all the fiscal resources it did not want to give back to the provinces -resources which, in fact, it had borrowed because of the war-and move into the field of university grants, contrary to section 93 of the constitution which gives the provinces exclusive jurisdiction in the field of education. In 1964, its range of action increased even more when it got into the field of student loans, and today, in another speech from the throne, it announces its intention to grant scholarships to students.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we, as legislators, will have once and for all to show sincerity of mind and away from the hustings, before everyone else, before the parliamentary correspondents and the third groups, before the troublemakers, assume our responsibilities and consider the problem boldly.
In the last few years, we have witnessed an increase in constitutional conflicts, conflicts which spread distrust throughout the country and push many Canadians further apart.
23033-26J
The Address-Mr. Allard
There are two points of view which must be understood. Personally, I respect both of them. English Canadians consider the fiscal and further constitutional definitions and centralization and uniformity of the economic or social legislation. Those people are satisfied with the political consultations instead of amending the constitution as required. I respect that opinion.
On the other hand, the French Canadian mentality demands the decentralization of powers and taxation fields, it asks for provincial autonomy, the particularism of Quebec and further constitutional definitions and guarantees in writing. Thousands of Quebeckers, thousands of French Canadians outside Quebec-according to the 1961 census, they number 1,298,000-who are also Canadians, are now giving serious thought- this is no joke-to the final direction of our political future.
They will choose between five political alternatives:	the status quo, co-operative
federalism, the formula of associate states, Quebec's independence and finally, a new Canadian constitution establishing throughout the country a positive and bicultural federalism and setting up in Quebec a special status in certain fields.
The status quo will not be accepted by Quebec and French Canada for three main reasons. First-and this is logical-conditions have changed since 1867 in the fields of economics, industry, natural resources and even culture. The fathers of confederation could not anticipate everything: surely, they could not foresee the invention of radio and television, the matter of rights over mining resources, in short they could not anticipate that conditions would change in time.
Second, the status quo is refused by Quebec and by French Canada because our past experience with federal and provincial governments has shown that the 1867 constitution was both weak and abnormal.
A true co-operative federalism should include the following ten features: independent and equal governments, clear and precise sharing of the powers of taxation, balance between the different governments, supremacy of the constitution, a constitutional court, recognition of biethnic and bicultural liberties and securities in the country, an amendment formula on fundamental problems acceptable to all parties, and Senate reform allowing provincial representatives to sit in that house.
396	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Allard
The text of the constitution of 1867 is not in line with the fundamental principles of true federalism which I have outlined. Ottawa's powers over provincial legislation are too great. The attribution of general legislative powers, the surrender to Ottawa of taxation powers, these are serious reasons why Quebec and French Canada want the constitution amended, reshaped and adjusted to immediate problems.
There is also the other option of co-operative federalism which has been tested in the last few years and which has shown that it would be limited to political consultations instead of providing a solution to the amendment of the constitution.
The associate states system is illogical. All Canadians are not prepared to accept this formula.
As far as the formula for Quebec independence is concerned, I think it is defective in three respects. First, no one-neither Mr. Bourgault, Mr. Chaput nor Mr. Jutras-has established that an independent Quebec would obtain more economic advantages on a long or short term basis.
Second, the formula is defective because an independent and separated Quebec would not, in my humble opinion, be in a position to help our 1,300,000 fellow-countrymen who are disseminated in the other Canadian provinces. Finally, a separated and independent Quebec would not be in a position to protect us from American penetration of our country by all possible means, that is, American magazines, television and radio.
What we need is a new Canadian constitution which will maintain what is good and essential and which will be based on necessary characteristics according to the aspirations of the two great nations and cultural groups. As members of parliament elected by the people, we have the responsibility to solve, as soon as possible, those economic, fiscal and constitutional problems.
A special joint parliamentary committee of the House of Commons and Senate should be set up during this session to consider all the reports of the various commissions, including the second report of the Laurendeau-Dunton commission on bilingualism and biculturalism, the reports and conclusions of the Carter and Belanger commission on taxation, and the findings which will be submitted in May, I believe, by the parliamentary committee, in Quebec, on the Canadian constitution. We should, here in this parliament, during this

DEBATES	January 28, 1966
session-1966 is a vital year for our country-look into all those reports, as legislators, and discuss them together.
It is very easy for us, Canadians, to fraternize, to converse nicely and politely with one another, but we should create, in addition feelings of friendship and brotherhood which would transform us into a dynamic nation, an example for all the nations in the world.
These are, Mr. Speaker, the few remarks I wanted to make this afternoon. If we, members of this twenty seventh parliament, act thus, we shall deserve well of the Canadian people, and we will be able to achieve unity in equality.

We must recognize that people in other categories have received consideration.
We all know that wages and salaries are moving upward. The people who are suffering most at the present time are those who are living on pensions and on fixed incomes, and unless we in parliament take the initiative in this respect we shall end up by not being very proud of the treatment accorded to those who have served in the public service of Canada in the years gone by.

Mr. Speaker, may I first congratulate you very warmly on your election to the office of Deputy Speaker and ask you to convey my congratulations to Mr. Speaker. I also wish to offer my congratulations to the new ministers and parliamentary secretaries.
However, I must admit in all sincerity that I deeply regret two departures from the cabinet, that of the former Secretary of State and that of the former Postmaster General. Having been the victims of a campaign of innuendos, they were tired and gave up their important posts. In losing them, we lost two economists. Fortunately, they will be able to serve their country as private members of the house.
I want to be brief today, because I promised the hon. member who will speak after me that I would give him the opportunity of delivering his speech and of visiting his riding during the week end, like all of us.
Much has been said about the Speech from the Throne in the press in general. It has been termed an important legislative program, which carries no surprises. For some, this document contains nothing new. Should legislation introduced by a government be reduced to surprise gifts? Must a parliamentary session have the suspense of a TV story? It has also been said that the sessional program was extensive, as expected. In my opinion, the volume of this program constitutes its greatest quality; it shows that the government has looked into several problems at a time.
Those who claimed that the speech from the throne contains nothing new probably meant that the legislation it announces has already been discussed. I would say, then, that in introducing these measures again, the government is not coming up with dangerous innovations. To those who say that there were no surprises in the Speech from the Throne, I want to say that there was at least one: the legislation designed to help agriculture in eastern Canada, a thing eastern farmers had long been waiting for.
Mr. Speaker, it is a great surprise and a great satisfaction for us who have read the Speech from the Throne. Let me mention as an example, the establishment of a Canadian Dairy Commission which, like the Canadian Wheat Board, will be invaluable for dairy producers, whether they live in Ontario, Quebec or the Maritimes.

Several pieces of legislation mentioned in the speech from the throne, for instance, the legislation to improve the movement and marketing of feed grain in eastern Canada and British Columbia will also be of great help to our farmers and will contribute to a reduction of their production costs, which will leave them with a much more interesting profit than in the past. Indeed, the eastern farmers and, in particular, the Quebec Catholic Farmers' Union, have long been asking for such grants for the transport of feed grain.
The measures dealing with increased capital for farm credit and unemployment insurance benefits for farm workers will also rejoice all farmers in my opinion. Those most important and necessary measures will be an efficient complement to the agricultural and regional development program which the province of Quebec has itself undertaken. It is the first federal session during which eastern farmers will receive at the same time an attention which seemed to be directed only toward the wheat producers. Indeed, the Quebec Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Alcide Courcy, is said to be very happy about the proposed farm legislation mentioned in the speech from the throne.
With regard to crop insurance, Ontario, Quebec and the Maritimes have, here again, long been asking for the application of that legislation. I recall that when I had the honour of sitting in the house from 1958 to 1962, the government of the day had initiated the crop insurance act. I remember rising in the house at that time to say that I appreciated that legislation, that it would certainly be of benefit to farmers but that, unfortunately, it could not apply in eastern Canada because of our diversified farming, whereas, in some provinces, it would be much easier to apply.
I am happy to see that the government has kept its election promise and that the Crop Insurance Act will be amended so that all farmers, not only those in a favoured region, will benefit from that legislation.
ARDA will also greatly help our farmers, thanks to an agreement reached with the provincial government. In my riding of Beauce we have been able to appreciate that legislation because most of the dredging operations carried out in the Chaudiere river, now famous for its floods, were undertaken under ARDA. According to statistics, the province of Quebec has, thanks to ARDA, completed 170 projects and it is expected that it will

continue to benefit from ARDA in the fields of farming and forestry and with respect to the tourist industry.
With regard to the purchase of unproductive and uneconomic farms, Quebec already has its own legislation, but the policy of the present federal government will be an encouragement to pursue its policy of regrouping farms and converting unproductive land to forests.

In an election campaign which is still fresh in our memory, we, on this side of the house, on behalf of the government, had said to our people that the policies we were presenting would enable them to conclude that the greatest concern of this government was protection for the farmer.

Besides, this agreement had been reached in July 1965 between the government of Canada and the Quebec government. It has been

During the election we talked about medicare. It was easy for us to talk about it. Another very important matter mentioned in the speech from the throne is that of university grants and student scholarships. I have already had the opportunity of saying here in this house, that our young people should have access to education, whether they are the sons of humble workers or farmers or rich financiers. I have said it is their inalienable right to acquire an education and that we should permit their fondest hopes to come true.
Of course, such legislation will require some co-ordination between the provincial and federal governments. Quebec will no doubt prefer the financial option.
A moment ago I heard the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) speak about "constitutional technicalities". Well, for my part, I say this: Let us grant such scholarships to the province of Quebec subject to option rights, and let us deal with the matter while students are already attending university. It is not desirable to prevent these students from attending university until such legislation is passed.
Should the education of one Quebec citizen or his access to university be delayed because of our- discussions on technicalities and our refusal to pass this legislation, we would cause irreparable harm to young people who are eager to learn and to fulfil their ambitions.
I believe the establishment of a Canada Development Corporation to promote investments in industry and the development of our natural resources is also a good thing. Certain parts of Canada, as we know, have few industries and this lack of organization is one

The Address-Mr. Racine of the causes of unemployment. I am very pleased that the present government has thought about that important problem. I am sure that that initiative will be an incentive to our industries and that it will create employment for our working class.
Since the beginning of the debate on the Address, all sorts of topics have been discussed. Some members asked for greater benefits under our social legislation, such as in the field of old age pensions; others suggested a raise in family allowances.

First of all, rest assured that I could hardly conclude this brief address without extending to my constituents of Beauce my heartiest thanks for the confidence they reposed in me on November 8 last. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the common good must come before the individual good. Mr. Speaker, my first words will be to thank Providence very sincerely and very humbly for electing you to preside over our deliberations; we heard so many good things about you and your assistants that I hope you all go straight to Heaven.
In this new parliament, like the speakers who have preceded me, I would like to make some remarks on the Speech from the Throne.
The Address-Mr. Latulippe
The speech from the throne contained all kinds of nice things indeed: the same promises, the same benefits, the same regulations or the same improvements contained in it three years ago when we set foot in this chamber.
In the throne speech this year we find exactly the same arguments as two and three years ago. I have therefore come to the conclusion that nothing has been accomplished, since the same things are coming up again.
The throne speech mentioned national unity. Canada will be united provided Canadians have an acceptable standard of living in a country overflowing with riches, and never otherwise.
There is talk of the war on poverty. Why have Canadian citizens become so poor? How come there is so much hardship in Canada when we always have had sound administrations, either Grit or Tory? A sound administration, they brag, it is now stated in the speech from the throne, that our country is enjoying an unprecedented period of prosperity and growth; that production, investment and trade have expanded rapidly; that Canada is making rapid strides; that employment opportunities have increased rapidly and that unemployment has decreased.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I think that if the people were doing so well, this would not be a topic. Where is the sincerity of those who tell us that the country is prosperous and then declare war on poverty?
This poverty was brought about, and deliberately so, by those who administered our country in the past; it was not wished for by the Creditistes who were not here at the time. It has been willed by those who administered our country in days gone by.
The Liberals governed us for 34 years out of 45 and the rest of the time it was the Conservatives.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, our previous administrations brought about unemployment, dire poverty, debts and bankruptcies of all kinds. Everybody is dissatisfied in Canada, and you have only to look around to see it. Why are the people dissatisfied? Why do people not even have the right to live decently? We empty the pockets of our citizens through taxation, we drain them dry and they are obliged to stay in their hovels; they cannot pay their rent because they have no money left.

January 28, 1966

The Address-Mr. Latulippe
Mr. Speaker, Canadians have had enough of this system. It is fine for those who are well paid. Canada, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) tells us, is prosperous. Prosperous, yes, for about 10 per cent of the population, for those who cater to high finance, who handle the funds. It is prosperous for loan companies. It is prosperous for companies listed on the stock exchange, because on the Montreal Stock Exchange around $2 billion of profits or income are made each month, while all the people in Canada do not make $2 billion of profits or income in a year. Some private citizens have to pay taxes, but not those who speculate.
Our production system is perfect, I congratulate those who administered us in the past for at least having organized well our production system. However, at the present time we are still saying that our production must be financed, that investments must be made to increase production, and in this field only, while we do not have anything to say as far as distribution is concerned. Our production is healthy, in fact, it is so healthy that in 1965 our production was worth $51 billion. Perhaps $35 billion worth has been sold, and it follows that from $15 to $16 billion worth could not be marketed. And yet those products were made for those citizens who need them. No investments are being made to foster distribution or to increase consumption. Then, if we want things to work smoothly, production should certainly be financed, but consumption too. In a country such as Canada where technological advances are commonplace, we will never succeed, Mr. Speaker, in creating unity, if consumption and the needs of our citizens are not taken into account.
At a time when our financial system is failing, we would like to amend it. Some people talk about finance, but Creditistes alone offer ideal solutions. All previous speakers, since the opening of the session, have asked and suggested all kinds of things, but there is no money to pay for them. None of those speakers have asked the government to put the printing press at the disposal of the citizens, none except the Social Credit members.
How shall we finance these things? By incurring debts? By continuing to borrow money and to empty people's pockets that have already been cleaned out? By paying $5 every time we receive $2 from the government? By the government withdrawing money from circulation instead of issuing new money? .

The system is basically wrong. It has to be reformed if we are to preserve our heritage, our family and our institutions. The Creditistes would urge the Bank of Canada to make interest free loans to producers, at a time when financial institutions have us under their heel, when we are fettered by grants, when farm credit puts us deeper into debt. All the government programs, the Industrial Development Bank, the Home Financing Plan, are all plans that put us deeper into debt for periods of 30, 40 even 50 years. Institutional grants tie up credit.
The Social Credit party would finance producers, farmers, public interests by way of interest free loans. We could finance highway construction and university building costs as well as the development of our natural resources. We could make investments intended for the development of our natural resources by means of Canadian credit. At present, Canadians go out of their own country to seek credit on foreign markets, credit that is granted with a stroke of the pen for the development of our institutions, of our natural resources; we pay interest to those foreigners and eventually we hand over the country to them.
It is a well-known fact that 80 per cent of our Canadian industries and natural resources are being developed and operated by foreign interests. So, if there is nothing in the Speech from the Throne to provide for all those things, it is up to us the Canadian people to assume our responsibilities and to reform things that are reformable.
Never mind what is satisfactory; there is not much to say about that. My constituency needs all kinds of things, just as all the other constituencies. It is a poor constituency, where farming is not very good. The government would have to spend several hundred million dollars to place it on equal footing with other constituencies. But if these millions are borrowed from high financial circles, we will get into deeper and deeper water and be in debt up to our necks.
Mr. Speaker, income tax is theft.
The national debt is nothing but deceit; the national debt should be converted into national funds, into social funds, into social credit.
The banks are taking away from Canadians the resources of Canada by entering them under "assets" in their books and under "liabilities" in the country's books. Under
January 28, 1966	COMMONS
their accounting system the banks convert to their own use the credit of society. They steal the social credit.
Interests on debts should be converted to social dividends. Thus, taxes would disappear and would be replaced by social dividends.
No one in the house, including the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker), the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), and all the other members, came forward with solutions to our Canadian problems, nor tried to balance the volume of [DOT]dollars and the volume of products. There is no equipoise; we are completely off-balance, and balance is only found in wartime.
Indeed, when we are at war, when products are needed, the necessary money is found, all budgets are easily balanced, every aspect of the economy is stabilized; but as for stabilizing at present the Canadian economy, it cannot be done.
And so, Mr. Speaker, the old parties system gave us poverty, bad debts, mortgages, mortgaged governments, bankruptcies, transfers of capital, repudiations of debts. Those are the things found in the present system. Instead of distributing the available and abundant production, we are satisfied with maintaining scarcity of money and high interest rates by implementing a money rationing system.
What are the solutions proposed for this problem? The Conservative opposition criticizes but offers no solution. The economy is stagnating instead of being developed. It is not allowed to expand.
We seek a solution from the economists, the best paid people to make plans and more plans to pull the wool over our eyes and lead us down the path of socialism because they claim the people are too ignorant to run things themselves. No one can run things when his pockets are emptied and barriers are raised to prevent money from entering into their pockets. Then, prominent citizens are called upon to solve the problem. This problem is not yet solved in countries where socialism is in power. Under socialism every one is in a quandary, everyone pays taxes, everyone is overtaxed. Most citizens of socialist counties cannot live like human beings. They live like animals.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Is that the system which is being forced upon us? In short, state socialism is advocated; there is a tendency toward the left, which is completely contrary to individual freedom.
