The Address-Mr. Latulippe
It is suggested to steal from those who have in order to give to those who have not, that is, to rob Peter in order to pay Paul, while the fine realities remain unsolved. Scarcity is simply being spread instead of wealth.
The system is basically wrong since it forces the country to produce more money than the system has created. That is spreading indebtedness everywhere. It is compelling people to fight among themselves to find the money required for an impossible joint operation. It is leaving the weak high and dry and compelling those who want to survive to be exacting; it is forcing public bodies to overtax for the system after taxing the services.
We must accept the evidence that the fault lies with the money system. The system does not work because it does not make the money; go any place where there are human needs.
In addition, what parties in power in this country in the last 50 years have manufactured a funny kind of money which is constantly depreciated and which has sent us from inflation to deflation, from crisis to economic stagnation, from economic depression to financial bankruptcy? Is it Social Credit, the Liberals or the Conservatives? That is what Canadians should know and remember.
Mr. Speaker, one of the great problems facing this government is the international balance of payments.
Reference has been made to this from the start of the session, but no solution was advanced to solve this problem, which arises from the Bretton Woods agreements. This is not surprising, because when the international monetary fund was established in 1944, under the Bretton Woods agreements, the old capitalist formula prevailed. Three big countries held between them a large majority of shares. Instead of creating an agency of control run by a few countries only, a quota of equal value should have been established for each country, or equal voting rights for all the members.
On July 9, 1956, Mr. Solon Low, then leader of the Social Credit party and member for Peace River, made the following statement:
"The Bretton Woods agreement favoured particularly creditor countries such as the United States without imposing on them the obligation of balancing their trade by having to accept products from other countries. However, it imposed this obligation on the debtor countries. It established
406	COMMONS DEBATES	January 28, 196S
The Address-Mr. Latulippe
an international gold standard and gave creditor countries the right to wait and demand gold or American dollars."
Here is the problem. As long as the Bretton Woods agreements remain, so will the problem.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the main cause of the balance of the international accounts problem. Unfortunately, those settlements were approved in 1944 by the Liberals, who were then in office and by the Conservatives and Socialists, who formed the opposition.
The Social Credit party, then headed by Mr. Solon Low, was the only one to be square against those harmful agreements. The developments which followed were to prove that only Social Crediters had known what they were talking about.
Those who, in this house or elsewhere, are saying that Canadians have enough purchasing power and that our monetary system is perfectly balanced are either decent people who are terribly unaware or blind, or men who are distorting the facts.
There are still a great number of officially unemployed people in this country-and by "officially" I mean those who are getting unemployment insurance benefits, heads of families receiving about $35 a week, which is shamefully inadequate considering the ever-increasing cost of living.
We have a lot more than this. Many citizens do not appear in the Unemployment Insurance records, but they are on social welfare. Social allowances are going to account for 25 per cent of the budget that is almost a billion and a half dollars for 1966. So that people are transferred from the Unemployment Insurance lists to social welfare lists. Under social welfare, they have to live on $25.00 to $35.00 per week. This is unthinkable in a country such as Canada which is extremely wealthy. One cannot realize that citizens can be allowed to live on such incomes. It is a shame.
Therefore it is important to do away with austerity programs and launch huge public works in the most affected areas, without levying additional taxes and without borrowing from the financial market. In other words, let us use new money. With this purpose, let us create immediately a social financing bank or a bank of social capitalization, directly connected with the Bank of Canada, but having the same authority to create credit as the chartered banks.

That bank of social financing should only lend money at a rate high enough to take care of administration costs.
Those are problems which should be dealt with in the house. As long as we do not settle the problem of finance, we will always witness the same disorder, the same disadvantages, debt restrictions, bankruptcies, debt increases for the taxpayers and for the government.
Only drastic measures will curb unemployment; the remedy is simple and painless. We must spend more; which is even more necessary, is increased expenditures in what is called the public sector that is, expenditures for public education, health, recreation, as well as for a variety of other services and facilities of which there is a great need in Canada.
Recently, I read in a magazine that within three years 20 per cent of our labour force will be laid off on account of automation and that the proportion will reach 30 per cent within five years.
We hear people talk about full employment but how can we provide jobs for everyone when mechanization and automation replace man. Full employment has become impossible. To that effect, I am going to tell you about an industry where production amounts to $15,000 a week and wages $1,500 a week.
Do you figure that the $1,500 wages will purchase the $15,000 production? Never, and that is the root of the problem. That is where those who talk of full-employment are talking through their hats because they do not realize the present situation. They do not realize that automation, mechanical and technical development are accepted in every field, and that they supersede manpower.
Men are born with needs. They must eat, learn, dress, find lodging, and that is the problem. That problem could only be settled through credit created by the Bank of Canada, or a board of control, or by balancing our financial resources, with our total marketed production available to our citizens.
The Federal Bureau of Statistics announced that the total debt of Canadian consumers reached, at the end of 1964, $4,552 million as against $4,422 million the previous year.
When those figures were released many newspapers explained that the increase in private debts stemmed from easy credit. It may be. This running into debt proves three things; Canadian consumers have needs; products exist to meet those needs; no money is
January 28, 1966	COMMONS
available to satisfy the existing needs. No matter how numerous they may be, no economists, of our home-grown variety or graduated from the London School of Economics, can deny this assertion.
Since Canadians had to resort to borrowing, it also proves that they cannot live without the permission of those who control money and credit.
If lenders want to create credit or money, needs can be met. But, on the contrary, if they refuse, consumers must tighten their belts. Therefore, they are faced with the following dilemma: either they run into debt or starve.
On the other hand, some people believe that consumers are in debt to finance companies, businesses and stores selling on an instalment system.
A small part of those debts is really due to finance companies, but most of the loans granted by finance companies or sales made on an instalment plan by businesses are financed by bank loans. Canadians are thus owing some billions of dollars to bankers who create credit.
To these billions owed by the Canadian consumers, we must add the billions owed by the Federal Government, the billions owed by the provincial governments, the billions owed by the municipalities, the billions owed by the school boards, the billions owed by those who mortgaged their homes and their farms. All in all, Canadians owe $86 billion which is equal to $4,600 per capita or $20,600 for the average family. And this, when the legal money issued by the Bank of Canada totals only $2,490,833,000. How is it that only $2 billion of legal money is put in circulation while we have a debt of $86 billion? This proves, Mr. Speaker, that somewhere there are false moneymakers who are as guilty as any counterfeiters of $20 or $10 notes. And nobody is doing anything about it. Laws protect those counterfeiters.
Financiers and masters of credit thus control governments. They are the ones who rule them with a rod of iron and who appoint their own creatures, like Kierans, to the key positions. There are many of them that I could name in this government. Those same financiers control the provinces, municipalities, towns, school boards, institutions, universities and schools.
Those who thus have the right of life and death over all institutions did nothing at all in order to build this country; nevertheless, the country belongs to them.

The Address-Mr. Regimbal
Those who toiled or are toiling, those who are building this country, who are manufacturing the products, the goods to meet our needs, they are enslaved, indebted and controlled.
The affluent people, the "controllers", the debt makers, are those who control credit, who manufacture credit in the form of debts.
It is the worst form of dictatorship. There is no need to go to Russia to find a dictatorship. We have one in Canada, a country which is supposed to be a democracy; a dictatorship controls all man's activities, holds the right of life or death over each one of us-

Mr. Speaker, before beginning my first speech in the House of Commons, may I express, within my humble means, the very deep feelings of pride and joy that your unanimous election to this responsible post and your gracious acceptance stirred in the hearts of all French Canadians, particularly among the French speaking minorities throughout Canada, and among the French people of Ontario who share with you the marks of respect and honour which have been bestowed upon you and which, everyone agrees, you fully deserve.
All the previous speakers pointed out your mastery of our two official languages. The success which has come to you because of your courage, determination and competence, should serve as an example and encourage all our French speaking compatriots to increase their efforts to maintain and develop that precious heritage, our French culture, and all our English speaking compatriots to increase their efforts to acquire, improve and master the French language, also their heritage as Canadians.
Maiden speech. Most of the members of this house have been through this experience, all can understand and relive the emotions and agitation I feel at this time.
I hasten to say, Mr. Speaker, that I am just like the others who speak here for the first time. Yes, I am impressed; yes, I am
January 28. 1966

The Address-Mr. Regimbal moved; yes, I am somewhat frightened. But having said this and being understood I shall proceed with my remarks.
First of all, let me congratulate the members for Dollard (Mr. Goyer) and for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) respectively mover and seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
I, too, am a newcomer. I only hope to survive this maiden speech with as much assurance and if I achieve half as much brilliance, it will be a great success indeed.

Everyone seems to agree that the Speech from the Throne underlines two facts very clearly. The first is that we have a lot of work to do in the months ahead, and I don't doubt for a minute that all of us intend to put our best efforts forward to do so in a commendable, efficient manner.
The second fact is that we are faced with a government which has failed once again to secure a majority. I intend to touch upon some of the possible reasons for this situation, but in the meantime, out of all this comes the very obvious note that the government does not have general support across the nation; that outside of Ontario and Quebec the Liberal party has 24 seats across Canada. Therein lies a heavy responsibility.
I suspect, from reading the Speech from the Throne, that the government, which received 40 per cent of the popular vote, as compared to the 32 per cent which the official opposition gathered, realizes that responsibility, and realizes that it must pay particular attention to the recommendations of the official opposition, and proportionately to those of the third party and the other parties.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The opposition was gratified to find indications of forthcoming legislation which was part and parcel of our program, for instance the increase of per capita grants to universities from $2 to $5. We trust that likewise the government must give due consideration to, and we will continue to press for, other urgent needs of the Canadian people as expressed by the opposition, such as the following:
First, $100 a month pension benefits to the aged. Even though the amendments went down to defeat, it is more and more obvious that most of the government members are as convinced as we are that the $100 pensions are the wish and the will of the very vast

majority of Canadians and that no government can expect to carry on if it deliberately ignores the will of the people.
Second, the same situation applies in our request for immediate recall of the 11 per cent tax on building materials and production machinery, and this too went down to defeat. In refusing to act on this, the government ignores the wishes of all the opposition and most of its own members.
Third, long overdue relief and attention to eastern farmers as pointed out by several hon. members in the past few days.
Fourth, deduction of property and school taxes up to $500 from taxable income. There again, government members have come out and joined in our request, and we intend to continue to press for this.
Fifth, the same applies to our policy of making old homes available for mortgages under the C.M.H.A. Surely the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), in his future role of minister of manpower will realize that in this day and age, more and more industrial employees, senior clerks, and junior executives are being transferred to other parts of the country and that the first effect of their move is to take a financial loss on their homes because, in spite of our great prosperity, there is no one around to buy who has the necessary down payment to cover the amounts which they have already poured into those homes.
Sixth, how can the government ignore the reasons behind our suggestion of a consumer loans act which would protect wage earners against the exorbitant interest rates having to be paid on loans directed to home improvements?
Seventh, if I can draw a page from my business background, I feel very strongly that this is the right time to introduce tax relief on personal income and on corporate income because the strait-jacket is beginning to hurt. The wage and salary earners cannot cope with further inflation and are forced to live beyond their means, and corporations do not have the proper incentive to conquer new fields and meet new challenges.
All of these, Mr. Speaker, are points which were in our program of policies for people, and were lacking in the Liberal party platform, which explains why 60 per cent of the people voted against that party. I think these policies are a credit to the Progressive Conservative party, and to our leader, who made
January 28, 1966

such an outstanding effort in bringing them home to Canadians in all corners of the country.
The opposition will also bring out the fact that two thirds of the government members represent urban and big city ridings and interests, so that particular care must be given by the government to agricultural and rural problems which might not get their fair share of attention. This could explain, for instance, why so many small towns have still not received their grants for 1964 winter works. Small towns = small problems = little or no attention.
At this point, however, I would like to insist on another job which has to be done, and which is every bit as important as all the legislation which will be introduced because it has something to do with the fact that this country has decided on another minority government. I insist, because we are all equally involved, and should all be interested, that there is an urgent need to restore the respect and prestige of parliament, and the image which we reflect in the minds of our citizens.
Before the election fever tapers off completely, while the thoughts and the qualms of our electors are still fresh in our minds, why do we not take into immediate account those few very timely pointers which all of our constituents have ever so humbly whispered into our ears, with the hope that we could do something about them, and that we should all agree that it should be done.
Throughout the campaign, in every nook and cranny, our people have talked and complained about morals, dignity and Canadian unity or the lack thereof. We owe it to ourselves and to all Canadians to give concrete evidence of our intention to improve our performance on all three points and, in so doing, restore the public confidence in parliament and parliamentarians.
Nobody expects miracles, but our whole population-our youth especially-is looking to us to set an example and to follow up words with action. Please do not judge my remarks as those of a do-gooder who cannot distinguish between fact and fiction. Besides, if ever any preaching has to be done, I would rather rely on my colleague, the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacDonald), who is an expert in this field. I repeat, these are points which our constituents have brought up and which deserve our attention.

Under the heading of morality, I am under the very clear impression, after this recent
The Address

Mr. Regimbal campaign and the profusion of scandals which preceded it, that our fellow citizens ardently wish that we would take specific action to show, in a practical way, not only a moral concern, but morality in our activities.
I am sure, for instance, that the majority of Canadians are unaware of the fact that we do have prayers at the opening of our sittings. Let us first say so to everyone.
I am sure that the majority of the members of this house are unaware of the contents of that prayer. Let us first learn it.
I am also sure that the great majority of our citizens do not know that we have in the parliament buildings a quiet place where the members can go to meditate, and I am sure that a great many members would not know how to find this place. Let us mention it, and then let us go there once in a while. Moreover, I am confident that if we do we will soon make up our minds to improve its surroundings for, frankly, it is neither suitable nor adequate. Now let us try to go one step further. Each one of us in his personal, family or professional life, sometimes feels the need for moral counsel. And yet here, where after all we are responsible for giving leadership to a whole country, this same need does not seem to be acknowledged. And yet, all the services necessary to discharge our duties are available to us.
May I make a digression here, Mr. Speaker, to insist on the excellent service we obtain from civil servants, security officers, secretaries, messengers, kitchen attendants, waitresses and staff members, and to pay homage to them all. However, I would suggest right now the establishment in the parliament buildings, on behalf of the members of the house and the whole personnel, of a padre service or chaplaincy, which institution proves so valuable in other fields of human endeavour. It will indeed be a new feature to have on the spot ministers whom everybody may fully and equally trust.

Under the heading of dignity, there are several areas where our performance is underscored, rightly or wrongly. I refer to such things as absenteeism, where I suggest that a roll call could be established as proper incentive for individual effort. In this connection one must consider the reading of newspapers during speeches and deliberations. I was happy to discover that in our party efforts are being made to tone down the practice. Finally
410	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Regimbal I would mention the practice of desk-thumping as a form of applause. I do not know where the solution lies, perhaps marble-top desks would be an idea; but I know that if we do find a solution, in the public eye we would come out of it ten feet tall.
Finally, as regards Canadian unity, most Canadians who have had the wonderful opportunity of visiting Canada from coast to coast, agree that the only thing wrong with Canadians is that they do not know Canada and do not know Canadians. I suggest that legislation be introduced which would provide direct financial encouragement to make It possible during centennial year for Canadians to see Canada by travelling throughout our beautiful country. A Canadian who has known the determination of Newfoundlanders, the industry of mari-timers, the colourful Latin character and charm of Quebec, the progressiveness of Ontario, those solid citizens of the prairies and the breathtaking grandeur of the Rockies, cannot help but feel big and proud for being an essential part of it all.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
So while the legislators, the intellectuals, the constitutional experts, are hammering out the legal, technical and inspirational problems involved in updating and Winging home our constitution, the average Canadian will be finding his own level on the basis of personal experience and knowledge, which after all is what the constitution is all about.
Where language differences exist, we will learn to understand these differences and to use them, cultivate them and preserve them, because these differences are what make us great and can be used to complement each other, to broaden our minds, to increase our knowledge and ripen our judgment. Our differences, like those between man and woman, can be used as an element of unity, of rapprochement, rather than divisiveness, so that we can all say-as was suggested two days ago-"Vive la difference".

In closing, Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to say that there is another tradition that at this time I wish to respect. I refer to the one whereby a new member making his first speech may praise the beauties and assets of his riding. But it would take too long to do justice to Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes in this respect. The attempt was being made at that time to work out the steps necessary to patriate the Canadian constitution, and a fairly large area of agreement was reached. As a matter of fact, we were on the verge of agreeing on a formula that would have been much more flexible than one which
The Address-Mr. Douglas the present government has been recommending. The discussions broke down on whether or not section 92 (13), which has to do with property and civil rights, should be entrenched.
Some of us took the position then-and I take the position still-that in view of the various court decisions relating matters of the marketing of agricultural products, labour legislation and social security measures to section 92(13), covering property and civil rights, it would be hamstringing Canada to agree to entrench that particular clause.
We believe that a Canadian constitution must be sufficiently flexible to give the federal government the necessary power to provide for equality of treatment and equality of opportunity for all Canadians, while at the same time recognizing a special status for the province of Quebec in terms of language, culture and the civil code, in keeping with the principle of the equal partnership of the two founding races.
We believe that a revision of the constitution should be based on four general principles, the first being that federal powers must be clearly defined to enable the central government to deal with the problems of economic growth, unemployment and economic dislocation. Some provinces may think they have the economic power to deal with these problems, and perhaps they are right, although I doubt it.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
There is no doubt about the fact that many provinces cannot cope with these problems. The federal government must have the power to equalize opportunity as between the various areas of Canada and remove, in so far as it is economically possible, regional disparities. It is an old saying that a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. If there is any part of Canada which is economically depressed, that will do more to destroy national unity than any other thing that might happen in Canada.
Second, we say that there must be a clear delineation of the provincial fields of jurisdiction, and the allocation of the necessary taxing powers to enable the provinces to discharge their responsibilities. The responsibilities which were given to the provinces under the British North America Act by the Fathers of Confederation, seemed to be relatively unimportant responsibilities in 1867. Today they are tremendous responsibilities, and with the growth in the demand for education,

412	COMMONS

This is a matter to which attention must be given in delineating not only the powers of provincial governments but the tax sources which they must have to discharge those responsibilities.
We say, third, that there must be a clear recognition of the special status of Quebec in respect of its language, culture and traditions. We think that such a status must be entrenched, but not in its present limited form. I envisage the day when our constitution will guarantee and ensure equal status of both languages throughout Canada. I look forward to the day when the constitution will guarantee the right of education in either English or French to every Canadian in any part of Canada. The status of Quebec, in terms of its culture, must be recognized as an expanding area, just as the cultural freedom of English speaking Canadians must be similarly recognized.
Fourth, we believe that a bill of rights should be written into the constitution and should also be entrenched. This bill of rights would guarantee to all groups of Canadians the basic freedoms-freedom of speech, the right of assembly, freedom of religious worship, freedom from arbitrary arrest, and all the other basic freedoms which we have come to associate with being part of British justice. We in this party, therefore, want to see a revised constitution. We want to see it domiciled in Canada. We want to see it have a flexible amending procedure. But, we have opposed the so-called Fulton-Favreau formula. Apparently we are now getting a great many supporters in this regard.

I think the statements made by the attorney general attending that conference were abundantly clear. We objected to the formula at that time because we believed it would put Canada in a constitutional strait-jacket. We contended then, as I contend now, that we need a constitution in which there is sufficient flexibility to deal with the problems of agricultural marketing, labour relations and the growing field of social security; that we must have the flexibility to deal with problems which will undoubtedly arise out of automation and technological change.
We were agreeable then, and we agree now, that some sections of the constitution, as I have already indicated, ought to be entrenched. The particular prerogatives and privileges that were given to the province of Quebec as part of the partnership in confederation, of course, have to be entrenched. The bill of rights ought to be entrenched. There are provisions which we agree should be entrenched; but the parts of the constitution

which have to do with the country's adaptability to meet changing, modern conditions, ought to be capable of amendment by at least two thirds of the provinces, provided they represent over 50 per cent of the population. We believe that the cultural dualism of this country demands the necessary flexibility to enlarge the cultural freedom of both English speaking and French speaking Canadians.
This, of course, would be impossible if any one province had the right to veto an amendment. It seems to me it is absurd to suggest that in a country as diverse as Canada, some amendment which is concurred in by both houses of the parliament of Canada and nine provincial legislatures could be prevented from coming into effect merely because one provincial legislature refused to agree.
When the present government came into office in 1963, the Quebec government of Premier Lesage apparently withdrew their objections to this formula. Now they dissent, but at that time they agreed. Saskatchewan was the only province objecting, and in 1964 when a Liberal government was elected in Saskatchewan they concurred. So that up until recently, and certainly since the Charlottetown conference, it looked as though all provinces would concur. Now Quebec has withdrawn its concurrence.

Apparently the premier of Quebec now recognizes that we were right in opposing the formula which would place Canada in a constitutional strait-jacket. Apparently he now recognizes that unanimity cuts both ways. It is significant that in his letter to the Prime Minister of January 20, this statement appears on page 2:
Thus I have always assumed that, as regards the amendment of legislative powers, any diminution of provincial power required unanimity, whereas any increase of such power called for the concurrence of only two thirds of the provinces representing one half of the population. This view, however, is not shared by everyone, even the specialists. It is contended, in fact, that under the formula any province could prevent the extension of the powers of another province.

No law made under the authority of this Part [DOT]affecting any provision of the constitution of *Canada that refers to one or more, but not all the provinces shall go into force unless it is concurred in by the legislature of every province to which the provision referred.

It is now clear to Mr. Lesage that if Quebec is to have cultural status and the cultural freedom to develop its traditions, then it must have a more flexible formula, just as some of the English speaking provinces recognize that if we are to cope with the economic problems of a technological age we must also have a flexible constitution.
However, Mr. Speaker, the most amazing conversion of all is that of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Favreau), who has been proposing this amending procedure. His name is now attached to it, along with that of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). He has been its chief protagonist. But last week, speaking in the city of Montreal, as reported in the Globe and Mail for January 22, he said:
I would rather delay the repatriation of the constitution-although, as everybody knows, I consider it essential-than see the reform of the constitution entrusted to a parliament dominated by the sentimental colonialism from which the Tories draw their conception of "national unity".
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, I think it is a sad commentary that the President of the Privy Council, the man who has been charged by the Prime Minister with the task of heading federal-provincial relations, when addressing a group of students, instead of pointing out to them the serious problems which confront Canada and the tremendous task ahead of us in trying to forge a new constitution to meet the needs of our day and generation, hides behind a cheap political gibe in which he sought to make the Conservatives the scapegoat for the fact that he had not been able to sell his formula even to his own native province.
As a matter of fact, what the President of the Privy Council was doing on January 21 in Montreal was simply administering the last rites to the Fulton-Favreau formula. But they had already been administered five days before by the premier of Quebec. Speaking in Montreal on January 17 Mr. Lesage said that things were moving so quickly in the country that a new constitution would be obsolete by the time it was written; and he considered that it would be dangerous for French Canada to insist that such a revamping be undertaken now.
So that on the 17th the premier of Quebec had already said that the Fulton-Favreau formula was dead; and on the 21st the President of the Privy Council administered the last rites to it. But on the 24th, three days later, the Prime Minister still did not know
January 28, 1966

The Address-Mr. Douglas that there had been a death in the family and proceeded to assure the house last Monday morning that the government intended to proceed with the amending formula.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, there is something wrong when the Prime Minister is not informed by his chief Quebec lieutenant that the latter, along with the premier of Quebec, have already decided that the Fulton-Favreau formula has been scuttled. And what is even more amazing is that the letter from Premier Lesage dated January 20 has apparently not been drawn to the Prime Minister's attention when he addresses this house on January 24. Surely, Mr. Speaker, we are witnessing government by trial and error, with error in the ascendancy. Surely there is something wrong when the Prime Minister of Canada stands before the House of Commons on a Monday to say that we are proceeding with an amending formula, and already three days before his chief Quebec lieutenant has said that it has gone out of the window, and three days before that the premier of Quebec has already indicated that he is not going to concur in it.
This government has become like a ship without a rudder. It is like a great ship wallowing in heavy seas with no one at the wheel. It reminds one of the old saying "Captain, art thou sleeping down below?"
The question now, Mr. Speaker, is: What is the government going to do in the light of what is happening? We in this party do not gloat over the scuttling of the formula, but we do believe we have been vindicated. We believe that the decision of the province of Quebec not to concur has saved Canada from taking a retrograde step. But this should not deter us from seeking to do what needs to be done and what the great bulk of Canadians want us to do, and that is to revise the Canadian constitution, to get it domiciled in Canada and capable of being amended in this country by the governing bodies of this country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are two theories about the constitution. There are those who have the "Let sleeping dogs lie" theory, those who say "Don't let's raise these thorny problems; if things get bad enough we will put another patch on the constitution and make another little amendment". This is the policy which has been followed for years. The result is that we have an outworn and obsolete constitution still domiciled in the United Kingdom.

The other concept is that we ought to revise our constitution in the light of modern needs and in keeping with the spirit of present day Canada; that a constitution ought to be a dynamic framework in which the people can work out their social, economic and cultural destiny.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
We in this party have been pleading with the government for a long time to have this whole question of revising the constitution referred to an all-party committee of the house. The constitution is not the sole prerogative of the heads of federal and provincial governments. We believe there is a need to ascertain the wishes of the people. We claim that parliament deserves something more than to be presented with a fait accompli after the federal government at a federal-provincial conference has worked out certain amendments and passed them on to the house without there being any opportunity for revision and change.
We believe that an all-party committee set up by this house should hear representations from people in all walks of life, all of whom will be affected by this constitutional question. It could consult with constitutional experts, meet with similar committees of the provincial legislatures, decide what things need to be revised and what things ought to be entrenched. Such a committee could isolate the points on which there continues to be disagreement.
It seems to us there is little value in talking about an amending formula until we revise the constitution. Until this is done we do not know what items parliament wishes to entrench and what items should be more flexible. Only when such a committee as I have suggested has reviewed the situation, worked out the areas of agreement and isolated the points of disagreement, would a national constitutional conference make sense. An all-party committee of this house would represent not only all the provinces of Canada but all the political parties in the provinces. There is in our opinion great value to be attached to the work which could be done by such a committee.
The view is sometimes held that constitutional arguments are for lawyers and that constitutions are not a matter of concern to the average citizen. We believe the constitution is a framework within which our society lives, moves and has its being. Again and again in our history our people have been
January 28, 1966

frustrated by restrictions and inhibitions placed upon them either by the constitution or by gaps in the constitution. All of us have had experience in days gone by of responsibility being passed from one government to another with regard to unemployment and a host of other questions, simply because responsibility for these matters was not clearly spelled out.
The people are concerned about the constitution. They should have an opportunity to express their opinions. Workers, farmers, university groups, businessmen, the legal profession-all these should have a part in revising the constitution, so that if this is to be a Canadian document to serve the future needs of Canada it will be forged by Canadians, as it ought to be, out of their experience and out of their history.
We do not think the dead hand of the past should be allowed to stay the onward march of progress. Human rights are sacred but constitutions are not. We believe it is possible under the direction of a parliamentary committee, followed by a constitutional conference on which all governments and parties would be represented, to work out a constitution which will serve the needs of the Canadian people. We believe it is not beyond the ingenuity of the Canadian people to safeguard and protect the rights which they now enjoy, and at the same time mould a constitution which will have sufficient flexibility as to make possible the onward march of our people toward a destiny which I believe is greater than any of us can possibly foresee at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I should like at this time to pause for a moment to thank very warmly the Greek communities of Ottawa, Montreal and Toronto, the order of Ahepa, for having sent me their congratulations and best wishes for success on the occasion of my election to this House of Commons. As you are probably aware, it happens that I am the first Canadian of Greek descent ever to be elected to the parliament of Canada, and this happened in a constituency which is almost 100 per cent French Canadian. This would indicate that in Quebec we are far from this fanaticism of which we have been accused. This is to the credit of my electors, whom I have the honour to represent.
Allow me to pay tribute particularly to the thousands of Canadians of Greek origin, and to the immigrants who add to our Canadian culture and contribute to the development of our resources.
Cradle of civilization and democracy, Greece has given to the world such great men as Socrates, Aristotle, Demosthenes and others who were famous philosophers and moralists. Canada is indeed justified in its pride of their contribution to the cultural and economic progress of the country.

Mr. Speaker, the riding of Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere is located on the north shore of the great St. Lawrence River, between the ridings of Joliette and Trois Rivieres. The inhabited portion covers an area 100 miles long and 50 miles wide and includes, at the northern end, an Indian reservation about which I will speak later on.
Mr. Speaker, it would not be exaggerated to say that approximately 75 per cent of the inhabitants of the riding are farmers. On their behalf, I would like to make known to the government the vital needs of the farmers who face enormous difficulties in the hard years we are going through now.
The uncertain weather of the last season only added to their misfortune. I know that the government intends to take a step in the right direction and adopt legislation to remedy that situation.
[Mr. Yanakis.l
DEBATES	January 28, 1966
I hail with great satisfaction the appointment of the member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) as Minister of Agriculture for the East. He is dynamic, a man whom we will be able to approach with our grievances. As we will soon be studying hopefully expected legislation to assist agriculture, mention of which was made in the speech from the throne, I should like to tell the house what suggestions farmers have made, the implementation of which would give them a ray of hope.
First, that farmers be granted more assistance with a view to increasing agricultural production, opening greater markets for their products and maintaining price levels which would enable them to reach a living standard comparable to that of the average worker, that is earnings of $4,200 a year.
Second, that a Canadian Dairy Board be set up to secure for our farmers an average income of $4 per cwt. for industrial milk, thus enabling producers of milk for processing to keep a close eye on prices, quotas, quality and exports of their products.
Third, that feed grain be supplied to farmers at reasonable prices through the storing of feed grain in eastern Canada.
Fourth, that a crop insurance program be set up to protect farmers against bad weather which sometimes ruins their crops.
Fifth, that a family head be allowed to pass on his farm to his children more easily when he retires; that his son or a close relative be given assistance for the purchase of a farm of his own and that the establishment of young farmers be made easier.
Sixth, that a larger number of development projects be subsidized through ARDA in the poorest rural areas to improve the welfare of those who depend on rural resources.
Seventh, that greater inducements be given to exhibitors of Canadian cattle. In that respect, Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to a very praiseworthy initiative of the young Canadian cattle breeders of Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere who hold an annual fair in the constituency. They should be allowed to stage class B exhibitions. To that end, a drive has already been launched to build an arena with all the required facilities for a regional fair. Provision should be made for long term loans for the construction of that building. That would be the best way to encourage those young breeders, to create a great deal of interest in this field and to have agricultural fairs play their part once again as the main educational centres for farmers.
January 28. 1966

Eighth, that the world food program be promoted through the purchase of powdered eggs by the government in order to maintain egg prices at a reasonable level.
Ninth and last, that the scope of unemployment insurance be enlarged so the main groups of full time farm workers could benefit from it.
Mr. Speaker, those are some of the challenges we will have to meet during this session. Farmers now find themselves in a tragic situation and it is our duty to get them out of the slump in which they have been for too long because of stagnant policies, both federal and provincial.
I promised them that I would take care of their problems during this session and I do not intend to go back to my riding with empty hands. By the way, I should like to tell the Minister of Agriculture that I accept with pleasure his invitation, which I received this week, to sit on the committee on agriculture. I think that perhaps that is where I can best serve the interests of my farming constituents.
Mr. Speaker, since my time is almost up, X should like also to point out the importance of my two counties from a tourist's standpoint. I may add that after agriculture, the tourist industry plays the most important part in the economy of the constituency.
The north of the county of Berthier, that is, the parishes of St. Gabriel de Brandon, St. Charles de Mandeville, St. Damien, St. Zenon, Ste Emilie, and St. Michel des Saints have beautiful scenery and ideal sites for vacationers. The same is true for the Maskinonge section, from St. Didace to St. Alexis des Monts.
Divine Providence gave this region magnificent mountains, entrancing panoramas, immense forests; hundreds of lakes dot the area for sportsmen and outdoorsmen to play and rest in an enchanting atmosphere.
The riding of Berthier-Maskinonge-De-lanaudiere, is located within 40 minutes of the metropolis, and can accommodate thousands upon thousands of summer residents. It is easily accessible by the Mont-real-Quebec Autoroute. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, these centers are not yet developed as they should be due to prohibitive costs of building parks, suitable vacation spots, camping grounds and access roads to the lakes. It would be timely, Mr. Speaker, to provide a tourist development plan and grants to municipalities that are anxious to develop their areas. This would provide employment

Another field which greatly affects the people is consumer credit. One only has to study the inquiry conducted last year in many families by the Caisses populaires and their representative, Mr. Laurin, to realize that several heads of families are in a very sorry plight, because when in financial difficulties, they grabbed the first hand held out to them by the finance companies, the loan shark outfits who, in the absence of proper legislation, exploit the consumer to the hilt.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, it is most urgent that we bring those exploiters back to reason by limiting their interest rates to the rates charged by banks and by prohibiting hidden costs, if we do not want to see the whole social fabric of our society ripped asunder.
Mr Speaker, I said a few moments ago that I would come back to the question of Indians. Indeed, my constituency includes an Indian reserve called "Manowan", which is a small village located 50 miles from the closest centre. Although the department sees to their education by providing schools and hospital services, those Indians live in a deplorable situation, having to share their houses with another family.
They do not have enough houses for the people living there. There are not more than 50 houses for a community of 600 people. Furthermore, there are no practical means of transportation, except by air. Hence the department should be authorized to build a road giving access to St. Michel des Saints, which is the locality nearest to their territory.
Mr. Speaker, before this twenty seventh parliament comes to an end, the Canadian confederation will have seen its hundredth anniversary. We are aware of the many problems dividing this nation at present and it is up to us to solve them.
The new dynamic Quebec of today wants to play a leading part in the development of a new and proud Canada. Canadians want us to speak in the name of Canada while fully respecting the rights of our two official ethnic groups, the English and the French. We must not be afraid to speak up and act with neither ambiguity nor provocation on the great problems of national unity and on the role that we, French Canadians from Quebec, must play in the running of the business of the nation. We must build a country which

The Address-Mr. Yanakis will plan to meet the challenge of the twentieth century. I fully agree with Sir Wilfrid Laurier when he said, and I quote:
The twentieth century belongs to Canada; therefore it is imperative for us all during the coming year, to build up our country, while safeguarding our moral values and our traditions, if we want to realize the great destiny which will be that of Canada on the eve of her centennial.
I would like to add, Mr. Speaker, that it is almost providential that we should have at this time as our leader, the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, a great diplomat who, faced with the serious problems of our time, has made tremendous achievements in the field of national unity. I am sure that his name will pass into history as one of the great prime ministers who has so well served his country.
I thank you for your patience, Mr. Speaker, and I hope these few remarks will receive from the government the consideration they deserve for the well-being of my constituents in Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere, whom I am proud to represent in this house.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND QUEBEC PREMIER RESPECTING CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT OFFICE OF THE PRIME MINISTER

speechtext:
Province of Quebec
January 20, 1966.
The Right Honourable
Lester B. Pearson, P.C.
Prime Minister of Canada Parliament Buildings Ottawa
My dear Prime Minister,
As is fitting upon the eve of a new session of the Legislature, the Quebec cabinet recently reviewed the principal items likely to be considered thereat. Among them are the draft bills entitled "Quebec Parliament Act" and "An act to provide for the amendment in Canada of the Constitution of Canada".
At the last regular session, the Legislative Assembly voted an address to Her Majesty, praying her to cause to be laid before the Parliament of the United Kingdom the bill entitled: "Quebec Parliament Act". This is linked up with the proposed constitutional amendment bill since the latter would have the effect of ensuring definitively to the only provincial upper House still in existence an absolute right of veto over any amendment of its own powers. Since the British parliament has not yet been seized of the request of the Legislative Assembly, the latter has not been called upon to consider the proposed formula for Eimending our constitution.
Many events have occurred since this formula was elaborated, and it would not be proper to ignore them. Among them should be mentioned the country-wide debate which has taken place respecting the formula itself, the continued dialogue between Quebec and the rest of the country, a constant and sustained evolution toward a new relationship between Quebec, the other provinces and the Government of Canada, the progress of the studies and discussions undertaken by the Tax Structure Committee, the Royal Commission of Inquiry on Bilingualism and Bi-culturalism and our own Special Committee on the Constitution.
You are also aware that the proposed formula for amending our constitution has caused some anxiety in Quebec. Whatever the cause of this feeling, it is a factor which should not be ignored. For instance, I personally am struck by the fact that, as early as last spring, the formula was not being interpreted everywhere in the same way. Thus I had always assumed that, as regards the amendment of legislative powers, any diminution of provincial power required unanimity, whereas any increase of such power called for the concurrence of only two-thirds of the provinces representing one-half of the population. This view, however, is not shared by everyone, even the specialists. It is contended, in fact, that under the formula any province could prevent the extension of the powers of another province. Needless to say, if that interpretation were to prevail, the evolution of our constitutional system in the direction desired by Quebec might become very difficult.
The visit which I recently had occasion to make to Western Canada also made me aware of the considerable difference between the manner in which Quebec wishes to see our constitutional system develop and the views held on this subject by many Canadians in other provinces. This difference of opinion, moreover, was confirmed to some extent by statements made after that visit by authorized representatives of other provinces. My feeling is that after this interval for everyone to ponder our country's future, we shall be in a better position to know what to aim for. It will also be most useful, in that regard, to reflect upon the work of the Tax Structure Committee and the forthcoming report of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism. By then, I imagine, each of the governments in the country will have had an opportunity to define its policy, not only in the field of federal-provincial relations, but also respecting the relations between French speaking Canadians and English speaking Canadians.

January 28, 1966
In the circumstances, the government of Quebec has decided to postpone indefinitely the consideration of the proposal for constitutional amendment.
Trusting that you will consider this decision as an indication of our sincere solicitude for the present and future progress of Canada, I remain, my dear Prime Minister, Yours sincerely,
Jean Lesage.

I have seen only today your letter of January 20 concerning t he Constitutional Amendment Formula. Stop. It raises a number of important and far-reaching problems of concern to the federal government and affects the situation relating to the action sought in London. Stop. My reply to your letter will have to be tabled immediately, yours is made public. Stop. In the circumstances you might think it best to defer making the contents of your letter public until you have had a chance to consider my reply which I shall try to send you immediately after consultation with my colleagues on Thursday. Ottawa, January 26, 1966 The Honourable Jean Lesage,
Prime Minister of Quebec,
Parliament Building,
Quebec, Que.
My dear Prime Minister:
As I pointed out in the telegram which I then immediately sent you, I saw only in the afternoon of January 24 your letter of January 20, 1966, concerning the constitutional amendment formula. The irony of it is that I had indicated that very morning, in reply to questions by the Leader of the Opposition and other members in the House of Commons, that the federal government had every intention to submit the constitutional amendment formula to Parliament as soon as it had been concurred in by all the provincial legislatures. I had thus implied that I remained of the opinion that Quebec would in due course endorse the proposed procedure to amend in Canada the Constitution of Canada.
My view was based on a number of positive factors which I could not but interpret in a positive and encouraging way, even though I was as you know fully aware of the difficulties.
First among those factors, of course, was the fact that the constitutional amendment formula was agreed unanimously by the heads of the federal and of the ten provincial governments at the Federal-Provincial Conference on October 14, 1964. We all then undertook to submit the proposed amendment procedure to our respective governments for formal approval following whatever procedure each thought appropriate. Secondly the White Paper which the federal government published on the subject in March 1965 had been endorsed without qualification by the ten provincial governments. Indeed, the Quebec authorities actively participated in the preparation of the French texts of both the amendment formula and the White Paper, and accepted them officially. The White Paper contained a detailed explanation of the various clauses of the amendment formula which was not questioned at the time.
Thirdly the Speech from the Throne, at the opening of the last session of your legislature, stated that: "So that the repatriation of the Constitution shall not have the effect of entrenching the powers of the Legislative Council over bills passed by the Legislative Assembly, you will be asked to restrict those powers". As a result, the Legislative Assembly eventually approved an Address to Her Majesty, praying Her to cause to be laid before the Parliament of the United Kingdom the bill entitled: "Quebec Parliament Act". For its part, the federal government has made a clear distinction, in deciding on the procedure that it should follow in advising the Governor General, between the Address approved by the Legislative Assembly of Quebec which relates only to the Constitution of Quebec, and the Address concerning the constitutional amendment procedure which relates to the Constitution of Canada. Your government, however, as confirmed in your letter of January 20, 1966, has maintained a direct link between the two proposals. Therefore I have to ask myself whether, as a matter of policy, the Legislative Assembly and the Government of Quebec would still wish the "Quebec Parliament Act" to be introduced in the United Kingdom Parliament.

Fourthly all the provinces, except Quebec, have formally notified the federal government of their formal concurrence in the proposed amendment formula. Undoubtedly in seeking the approval of their respective legislatures and in giving formal approval to the formula they shared my confidence that the Government of Quebec would take a similar step.
Finally, the federal government has all along been conscious of the potential relationship which exists between the amendment procedure and eventual revision of the Constitution itself. The studies mentioned in your letter as likely to have important implications for the constitutional development of Canada, were initiated before or concurrently with the approval of the amendment formula. The Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism was established in July 1963; the Special Committee on the Constitution of the Legislative Assembly of Quebec was created in June 1963: and the terms of reference of the Tax Structure Committee were agreed on October 14, 1964, immediately before the Federal-Provincial Conference also unanimously approved the constitutional amendment formula itself. Those are not therefore entirely new developments. Frankly, I had assumed that since the constitutional amendment formula represented, from the point of view of both the federal government and the provincial governments, such a marked improvement over the existing procedure in enabling us at last to amend our Constitution in Canada without having to go to the Parliament of another country, that the eleven governments would be prepared to accept it. But I certainly never excluded the possibility that, as part of an eventual revision of the Constitution, the amendment
procedure itself might then have to be modified to respond more effectively to any new federal-provincial relationship that might by then seem wiser or sounder for the achievement of constitutional change in the future.
In conclusion, I am bound to express my great disappointment with the decision of your government to postpone indefinitely the consideration of the proposal for constitutional amendment. I venture to hope that the Government of Quebec might be prepared to reconsider its decision in the light of the hopeful circumstances to which I have referred and of the many developments in the last three years in the field of Federal-Provincial relations. At the same time, I fully accept, of course, the expression of your "sincere solicitude for the present and future progress of Canada" contained in the closing paragraph of your letter of January 20, 1966. It is as a step in that progress and as an instrument for its continuance that the Government of Canada had hoped to see the amendment formula approved.
It is clear that, if your government does not consider that it can alter its position, we shall have to discuss the whole matter again at a future meeting of the Federal-Provincial Conference. Meanwhile, the position of my government remains as stated in that part of the Speech from the Throne opening the current session of Parliament, which reads: "It remains the objective of the federal government to provide that the Constitution of Canada may be amended in Canada".
Yours sincerely,
L. B. Pearson
Monday, January 31, 1966
